If someone calls any bet with any pair, bet your strong hands as large as they will call and do not bluff. If someone folds to every large bet, bluff large and bet small for value. Balanced sizing protects you against experts. Against everyone else, the most profitable size is the one that takes advantage of the specific mistake they keep making.
The real cost of anything

The cost of a choice is not only the money it takes. It is the best alternative you gave up to make it. Economists call this opportunity cost. An evening at the cinema costs the ticket and whatever else you would have done with those hours. A year at university costs the fees plus the salary you did not earn. Because the alternative never appears on a bill, people habitually leave it out of the reckoning.
Money has alternatives

Every dollar can be used once. Spending 5,000 dollars on a holiday means not investing it, not paying down a loan and not buying anything else. That does not make the holiday a mistake. It means the proper comparison is between the holiday and the best other use of the money. Businesses apply the same test when they ask whether a project earns more than the funds could earn elsewhere. A profitable project can still be the wrong one.
Time works the same way

Time is more limited than money, so its opportunity cost is higher. Saying yes to one commitment is saying no to whatever else could have filled those hours. A person who drives across town to save 10 dollars has sold an hour for 10 dollars, whether or not they see it that way. Working out roughly what an hour of your time is worth to you makes many small decisions about queuing, repairing and bargain-hunting much easier.
Free is not free

Things with no price still have a cost. A free concert costs the evening. A free sample costs your attention and perhaps your email address. Storing an unused item costs the space and the money you could have had by selling it. The useful question about anything is what you are giving up to have it. When the honest answer is nothing you would rather have, the decision is easy.
Sunk costs

A sunk cost is money or effort already spent that cannot be recovered whatever you do next. Rational decisions look only forward, at the costs and benefits still to come. What has been spent is the same under every option and should not affect the choice. People find this very hard. Having paid for something, they feel obliged to use it, and having started something, they feel obliged to finish, to avoid admitting the earlier outlay was wasted.
The fallacy in action

You have paid for a ticket to a show, and on the night you feel ill and do not want to go. The money is gone either way. The only live question is whether the evening would be better spent at the show or at home. Yet many people go, to get their money's worth. Companies do the same with failing projects. Britain and France kept funding the Concorde airliner long after it was clear it would never repay its costs.
How to catch it

A reliable test is to imagine arriving at the situation fresh. If someone handed you this half-finished project today, at no cost, would you choose to put in what is needed to complete it? If you did not already own this share, would you buy it at today's price? If the answer is no, the past investment is the only thing holding you there. Phrases such as we have come too far to stop now are a warning sign.
Using them together

The two ideas are partners. Sunk cost reasoning tells you to ignore what cannot be changed. Opportunity cost reasoning tells you what to compare instead: the best available use of your remaining money and time from this point on. Together they amount to one instruction. Look only forward, and compare the option in front of you with the best alternative, not with nothing and not with the past.
The goal

In May 1961, President Kennedy asked Congress to commit the United States to landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely before the end of the decade. At that moment the country had fifteen minutes of human spaceflight experience. The programme that followed, Apollo, employed around 400,000 people at its peak and cost roughly 25 billion dollars at the time. On July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed while Michael Collins orbited above.
Why a computer was needed

Navigating to the Moon and landing on it required continuous calculation that no crew could do by hand. The spacecraft had to know its position and speed, fire its engines at exact moments for exact durations, and during landing adjust the thrust many times a second. Ground control could help with navigation in flight. The descent to the surface, with a radio delay of over a second each way, had to be controlled on board.
The machine

The Apollo Guidance Computer was designed at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. It weighed about 32 kilograms and drew about as much power as a light bulb. It had roughly 2,000 words of erasable memory and 36,000 words of permanent memory. The astronauts communicated with it through a numeric keypad, entering two-digit codes for verbs and nouns. There was one in the command module and one in the lunar lander.
Woven memory

The permanent memory was literally woven. Each bit was stored by passing a wire either through or around a tiny magnetic ring: through for a one, around for a zero. Workers at a factory, many of them women with experience in textiles, threaded the wires by hand, following the program. Once made, the memory could not be altered. The software therefore had to be finished and thoroughly tested months before each flight.
Chips

The computer was among the first to be built from integrated circuits, the newly invented chips that put several transistors on one piece of silicon. In the early 1960s, the Apollo programme was buying a large share of all the chips made in the United States. That demand helped manufacturers improve reliability and bring down costs, which in turn hastened the growth of the industry that later produced personal computers.
The software

The programs were written by a team led by Margaret Hamilton, who promoted the term software engineering to give the work the standing of other engineering disciplines. Her team designed the system to assign a priority to every task. If the computer was asked to do more than it could, it would abandon the least important jobs, restart and resume the vital ones. Few computers of the day had anything like this.
The alarms

During the descent of Apollo 11, the computer began flashing alarm codes the astronauts had never seen in training. A radar left switched on in an unneeded mode was flooding it with useless data, and it was overloaded. Exactly as designed, it dropped low-priority work and kept flying the landing. An engineer in mission control recognized the code and judged it safe to continue. The decision to go on was made within seconds.
The landing

The automatic guidance was bringing the lander down toward a crater strewn with boulders. Armstrong took partial manual control and flew onward to find level ground while the fuel ran low. He set down with well under a minute of fuel remaining before a mandatory abort. Twelve people walked on the Moon between 1969 and 1972. Each of those landings depended on a computer far weaker than the one in a modern washing machine.
